# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Associative forward blocking[^1] refers to the attenuation of learning
about a stimulus-outcome relationship when the stimulus is accompanied
by another one that has already been established to reliably predict
that outcome [@beesley2011; @paskewitz2020].

[^1]: Herein, I will refer to forward blocking simply as *blocking* to
    avoid text cluttering. However, note that other forms, such as
    backward blocking, whereby learning stages of are reversed starting
    with compound cues followed by single-cue contingencies, were also
    defined.

Behavioural studies combined with eye-tracking have demonstrated that
blocking occurs in human associative learning and that it can be
accounted for by learned *in*attention to the blocked cue
[@kruschke2005; @beesley2011; @lepelley2007; @wills2007; @luque2018].
Two candidate mechanisms have been proposed to explain this phenomenon:
rapid **attentional shifts**, whereby redirecting attention away from
the blocked cue improves learning, and **attentional competition**,
whereby cues vie for a limited attentional resource [@kruschke2005;
@paskewitz2020].

However, no definitive experiment capable of discriminating between
these two proposed mechanisms has yet been conducted. Using simulations,
@paskewitz2020 derived an experimental design that could, in principle,
adjudicate between the two accounts.

The primary aims of this project are to:

1.  *replicate* the prototypical blocking findings of @beesley2011 in a
    large sample, and
2.  *design and implement an extension* of this paradigm that allows for
    direct comparison between the attentional shift and attentional
    competition accounts of blocking, drawing on the theoretical
    analysis by @paskewitz2020.

## Forward Blocking {#sec-history}

Blocking was first described in rodents by @kamin1969 and later
demonstrated in human contingency learning by @dickinson1984 and
@shanks1985. The basic phenomenon can be explained by simple associative
learning models such as the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972].
However, subsequent work suggested that blocking is accompanied by
shifts of attention away from blocked cues, and can thus be better
explained by attentional theories of associative learning [e.g.,
@mackintosh1975; @pearce1980].

Although alternative explanations based on propositional reasoning have
been proposed ***(cite propositional theories)***, learned attention
accounts remain influential and continue to be used in both empirical
and computational work [@paskewitz2020; @paskewitz2023; @kelly2025a;
@kelly2025b][^2]. Rather than adjudicating directly between competing
theoretical frameworks, the present study focuses on subjecting learned
attention models to a severe empirical testing [@mayo1991].

[^2]: **Look for more broad use of the theories. It is surely there,
    they are popular.**

Evidence for attentional mechanisms in blocking comes from several lines
of inquiry, including experimental manipulations of cue competition
[@lepelley2007; @beesley2011], eye-tracking studies of overt attention
[@kruschke2005; @wills2007; @lepelley2007], behavioural measures of
attentional bias [@liu2013; @luque2018], and computational simulations
of attentional learning models [@kruschke2005; @paskewitz2020;
@paskewitz2023; see also @sewell2012]. Building on recent simulation
work [@paskewitz2020], the present study designs an experimental
procedure aimed at testing key predictions of learned-attention theories
about blocking and its relation to attention.

## Computational modelling {#sec-computational-models}

Blocking elicited by the canonical blocking experimental designs can be
explained by *standard* associative learning models without attentional
components. For instance, @sewell2012 showed that when fitting the EXIT model
[@kruschke2001] to data from the canonical blocking paradigm (see
@tbl-design-01), the best-fitting attention parameters shrank toward zero,
effectively reducing EXIT to the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972]. In other
words, the canonical forward blocking can be accommodated without invoking
attentional mechanisms, even when such mechanisms are formally available
within the model [however, cf. @liu2013].

By contrast, *attention* is a necessary mechanism for associative models
to account for blocking elicited by a more complex three-stage paradigm.
@paskewitz2020 showed that within this type of paradigm, the EXIT model fails
to reproduce blocking unless it includes at least one attentional mechanism
(either rapid attentional shifts or attentional competition). Critically, when
these mechanisms are combined, the model becomes overly flexible. Unlike its
single-mechanism submodels, the full model can generate both the empirically
observed pattern as well as its reversal.

Rapid attentional shifting and attentional competition are thus best
viewed as competing explanations of blocking, rather than complementary
components of a single process. @paskewitz2020 propose a modification of
the three-stage blocking paradigm designed to differentiate between
these two accounts. However, empirical tests capable of doing so are
still lacking.

## Reproducibility of the effect

In the animal learning literature, blocking is widely regarded as a
cornerstone phenomenon, prompting strong claims such as that *"\[n\]o
empirical finding in the study of animal learning has been of greater
theoretical importance than the phenomenon of blocking."*
[@williams1999] However, despite its apparent robustness and the large
body of supporting evidence, @maes2016 were unable to detect the effect
across fifteen replications of previously published rodent paradigms
(see @soto2018 and @maes2018 for discussion of the implications of these
findings). Given this elusive nature of the blocking phenomenon even in tightly
controlled animal studies, it follows that any attempt to extend blocking
paradigms in human contingency learning should be preceded by a rigorous
replication of the original effect.

## Current study

Given the importance of both forward blocking as a phenomenon and attentional
mechanisms as a critical component of the associative models explaining it,
this study aims to experimentally decide between the two primary attentional
mechanisms of these models. In Experiment 1 we conduct a large-scale online
replication of the original @beesley2011 results, to ensure the effect's
replicability in the online environment and provide reasonable effect size
estimates. Subsequently, Experiment 2 adjudicates between rapid attentional
shifting and computational competition accounts of blocking, and Experiment 3
tests its conclusions in formally identical study design with different task
type.

# Experiment 1 (replication) {#sec-online-replication}

Although blocking is often treated as a single phenomenon, it can be
elicited using several related but methodologically distinct
experimental designs. These designs differ in how they set up cue
competition, control for confounds and what inferences they permit about
underlying mechanisms. @tbl-design-01 summarises two representative designs used
in prior research [@lepelley2007; @griffiths2009; @beesley2011].

```{r}

  "Standard"   , "C",  "-", "CD",  "+",   NA,   NA,  "D", "?",  "+",
  "Standard"   , "E",  "-", "EF",  "-",   NA,   NA,   NA,  NA,   NA,
  "Three-stage", "A", "o1", "AB", "o1", "BK", "o3", "BT", "?", "o4",
  "Three-stage", "C", "o1", "CD", "o1", "DN", "o4", "DQ", "?", "o3",
  "Three-stage", "E", "o2", "EF", "o2", "FQ", "o3", "FN", "?", "o4",
```

The **standard blocking design** [e.g., @wills2007; @liu2013; @spicer2021]
captures the core logic of the phenomenon. In the elemental training Stage 1, a
(*blocking*) cue A is established as a reliable predictor of an outcome
(designated by the A &rarr; + contingency in @tbl-design-01). At the same time,
the participants learn that another cue C does not predict the outcome
(C &rarr; -). In the subsequent compound training Stage 2, A is presented in
compound with a novel (*blocked*) cue B, and D is presented in compound with a
novel (*control*) cue C. Both compounds AB and CD are predictive of the outcome.
Although B is thus a valid predictor of the outcome, it is redundant because A
already fully predicts it. In a subsequent Test stage, participants are
typically asked to evaluate predictive value of all presented cues. Participants
typically rate B as less predictive of the outcome than D despite having the
same statistical contingency with the outcome. This difference is what
constitutes the canonical blocking effect.

Several limitations of the standard blocking design motivated researchers to
construct its alternatives. Firstly, since blocking cue A and its control
counterpart C are coupled in Stage 1 with different outcomes, the design cannot
differentiate between blocking due to relatively decreased rating of the blocked
cue B and relatively increased rating of the control cue C [@chapman1991]. A
commonly used alternative of the standard design omits presenting C in Stage 1
[e.g., @kruschke2005; @sewell2012]. While this change controls for the
confounding effect of Stage 1 training, it is partially confounded by **cue
novelty**. Specifically, the blocked cue B is introduced alongside a
well-established predictor (A), whereas the control cue D is paired with another
novel cue (C). This asymmetry makes it difficult to determine whether reduced
learning about B reflects blocking per se or differences in how novel cues are
processed within a compound.

A further limitation shared by both designs is that blocked and control
cues are consistently paired with the same outcomes. While this allows
for strong conclusions about specific cue–outcome associations, it
provides limited insight into **cue-specific processing**. In
particular, blocking effects observed in these paradigms may arise from
interference of cue-outcome associations (e.g., A-o1 interfering with
B-o1 learning or memory) without requiring any change in the processing
of the blocked cue itself.

To address these issues, @lepelley2007 introduced a **three-stage**
design in which both blocked and control cues are subsequently paired
with novel outcomes in novel training Stage 3, in the absence of previously
trained competitors. This modification has two important consequences. First,
it attenuates the novelty confound. Because all critical cues are paired with
new outcomes in Stage 3 and have comparable prior exposure, differences in
learning are less readily attributable to novelty. Second, and more importantly,
the design provides a more severe test of attentional accounts. By requiring
previously blocked and control cues to support new learning, the design creates
conditions under which any deficit in processing of blocked cues must generalise
beyond the original contingency. Consequently, this type of "novel learning" is
assumed to reflect cue-specific attention learning rather than direct
cue-outcome associative one [e.g., @lepelley2007; @griffiths2009; @beesley2011;
@uengoer2018]. The three-stage procedure was also used to evaluate mechanisms of
blocking by @paskewitz2020, making it a natural design choice for experimental
testing of attentional accounts of associative learning.

Accordingly, we first aim to replicate the findings of @beesley2011 and
then extend their experimental design following modifications proposed
by @paskewitz2020. Because these modifications concern behavioural
predictions and do not directly involve eye-tracking, we focus initially
on replicating and extending behavioural patterns of the three-stage
blocking paradigm. This approach allows us to leverage online sampling
to substantially increase statistical efficiency before moving to more
controlled laboratory studies.

## Method

### Participants

***Participants were recruited from the LABELS pool of Charles University
students enrolled in ... and tested online via JATOS (<https://www.jatos.org>).***

Sample size was estimated *a priori* following a power analysis based on
previously published results and a feasibility pilot study ()

### Procedure

In this study, we closely follow the procedure used by @beesley2011,
which was a variant of the allergy prediction task [@dickinson1996; 
@lochmann2003]. Each trial consisted of presenting a case of a
fictitious patient taking a vitamin pill containing certain chemicals
(*cues*) and asking the participant which of two possible side effects
(*outcomes*) the patient would suffer.

The overall study design followed the three-stage paradigm shown in the bottom
of the @tbl-design-01, with chemicals randomly assigned to cues *A*-*&beta;*,
and side effects randomly assigned to outcomes *o1*-*o4*, independently for
each participant. Critically, not only did the outcomes change between Stages 2
(compound learning) and 3 (novel learning), but Stage 3 also introduced a new
patient, Mr. Y, replacing the previous patient, Mr. X.

Stages 1–3 consisted of 10, 8 and 6 blocks, respectively, with each
block containing one instance of each of the eight stage-specific trial
types. Trial types were randomised independently for each participant
within each block, with the constraint that no trial type could be
repeated consecutively across block boundaries.

During the training stages (Stages 1–3; elemental learning, compound learning,
and novel learning, respectively), participants received immediate feedback
about the correctness of their responses to facilitate learning. In the test
stage, participants were presented with two chemicals and first selected the
side effect they believed the patient would suffer, followed by a confidence
rating for that judgement. No feedback was provided during the test stage.

### Stimuli

Cues (letters *A* to *&beta;* in @tbl-design-01) were randomly assigned names of
28 fictitious chemicals, separately for each participant. Because @beesley2011
do not provide a full list of chemicals used in their experiment, we used the
available list from @lepelley2007, which employed a similar three-stage
paradigm. As in @beesley2011, the following four side effects were randomly
assigned to outcomes, separately for each participant: dizziness, itchiness,
headache, and nausea. Outcomes *o1* and *o2* were always paired with Mr. X,
whereas outcomes *o3* and *o4* were paired with Mr. Y.

Cue stimuli consisted of words accompanied by a flask icon presented at
the top of the screen. Each training trial displayed either a single,
horizontally centred chemical name (Stage 1) or two chemical names presented
side-by-side (Stages 2–3), separated by ***some number of pixels*** and joined
by a horizontally centred "&" symbol indicating a compound cue. The left–right
order of cues in Stages 2–3 was counterbalanced within participants across
blocks.

At the vertical midline, a prompt reading *"Which of the following reactions did
the patient have?"* was displayed, followed by the instruction *"Click the
picture of the reaction that you think, then click the OK button"* on the next
line.

At the bottom of the screen, two images of the same patient (Mr. X in
Stages 1–2; Mr. Y in Stage 3 and the Test stage) were presented, each depicting
one of the two possible side effects corresponding to the outcomes. The
left–right mapping of outcomes was fixed, with outcomes *o1* and *o3* always
presented on the left and outcomes *o2* and *o4* on the right. An OK button was
displayed between the two images, centred horizontally.

Participants selected their response by clicking on the image corresponding to
the side effect they believed the patient would suffer. Upon selection, the
chosen image was highlighted with a thin black frame. After confirming their
choice by clicking the OK button, the response was recorded.

During training stages, feedback was provided immediately after each response.
The word "Correct" (in green) was displayed following correct responses and
"Wrong" (in red) following incorrect responses, replacing the OK button. The
correct response was additionally highlighted with a thick blue frame.

In the Test stage, responses were collected in the same manner, but no feedback
was provided. Instead, after each response, participants were asked to rate
their confidence on a scale from 1 ("Not confident at all") to 10 ("Very
confident"). Each Test block was presented six times in random order, with
left-right configuration of cues counterbalanced independently for each
participant.^[Note that this marks a departure from the @beesley2011 study,
which included a single Test stage block. However, the addition of Test stage
repetitions allows for more thorough effect estimation without interfereing
with the design being replicated.]

### Measures

#### Primary measure

In the standard blocking design, the following *blocking index* is typically
used to estimate the effect:

$$BI_1 = \mathbb{E}[(P(o1|C)-P(o2|C))-(P(o1|B)-(P(o2|B))]$$ {#eq-bi-1}

where $P(y|X)$ indicate judgement likelihood of outcome *y* given cue *X*,
positive values indicate blocking, higher values indicate higher magnitude of
blocking, *B* and *C* represent all blocked and control cues, and *o1* and *o2*
represent outcomes associated with control and blocked cues, respectively.

Another way, that is arguable more powerful in detecting blocking
[@griffiths2009], is to present in the Test stage cue compounds that pair
blocked and control cues that were associated with different outcomes during
Stage 3, leading to a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) procedure used here.
Adding the confidence rating, @beesley2011 computed the following blocking
index:

$$BI_2 = \mathbb{E}[Conf \times (I_{\{o2\}}-I_{\{o1\}})]$$ {#eq-bi-2}

where *Conf* represents confidence rating on each trial, *I~{y}~* represents
indicator function evaluated at participants response *y*, *o2* represents
outcome option associated with the control cue, *o1* represents outcome option
associated with the blocked cue, positive values indicate blocking, and higher
values indicate higher magnitude of blocking. Given the fact that BI~2~
comprised the estimate of the study under replication, it constitutes the
**primary response** of Experiment 1.
